text: [clean] Pinch off the lower leaves of vines to improve air flow between the stems.
[clean] Mix perlite or vermiculite into seed compost (roughly one part in four) to improve drainage for fine-rooted seedlings.
[clean] Keep a garden diary (sowing dates, rainfall, first frosts, yields) for every season.
[clean] Edge the lawn neatly each month so grass does not creep into the flower borders.
[clean] Plant a few tall sunflowers at the north end so that they do not shade shorter crops.
[clean] Keep soil pH (measured with a soil kit) between 6.0 and 7.0 for most vegetables.
[cool] Start by testing the soil pH and amending it before sowing the first seeds.
[cool] Plant spring bulbs (tulips, daffodils, alliums) at three times their own depth.
[cool] Start seeds indoors about six weeks before the last expected frost.
[cool] Add coarse grit to heavy soil to improve drainage.
[cool] Collect rain in barrels during wet months so the garden has a reserve.
[cool] Keep the soil around blueberries always acidic (pH 4.5–5.5) with ericaceous compost and collected rain.
[examine] Pull weeds while they are still small so they never set seed across the garden.
[examine] Keep newly sown rows moist until the seedlings emerge, because a single dry day can kill germinating seeds.
[examine] Grow tall crops on the north side so that nothing shades the shorter rows.
[examine] Prune raspberry canes to the ground after they fruit, and tie in the new canes for next year.
[examine] Once the garlic tops fall over, lift the bulbs and cure them in a dry, airy, shaded spot for weeks.
[examine] Once the pods swell, pick peas every other day to keep the vines producing.
[heat] Build a compost heap at least a meter wide so that it decomposes rapidly and evenly throughout the year.
[heat] Keep a bare ring so grass does not compete for moisture and nutrients.
[heat] Prune fruit trees in late winter while the branches are still bare.
[heat] If the leaves turn yellow, test the soil before adding any more fertilizer to the patch.
[heat] If aphids cluster on shoot tips, rub them off between finger and thumb.
[heat] Mark where bulbs are buried so they are not dug up later in the year.
[put] Avoid planting the same crop family in a given patch more than once every three years.
[put] Choose disease-resistant varieties for crops that suffered blight, and record how each variety performed.
[put] Pick courgettes often while they are small and tender, as large ones lose flavor.
[put] Before buying new shrubs, study how much sun and shelter each corner of the garden receives.
[put] Sow carrots, parsnips, and beetroot thinly in drills 1–2 cm deep from March to June.
[put] Rotate the four main groups (legumes, brassicas, roots, alliums) around the plot to break pest and disease cycles.
[puttwo] Cover brassica seedlings with fine insect-proof mesh (0.8 mm or smaller) straight after transplanting to exclude cabbage white butterflies and flea beetles.
[puttwo] In early spring, before the buds break, prune bushes into a goblet shape so that air moves freely through the branches.
[puttwo] Sow hardy annuals directly where they are to flower and thin them to about a span apart when they are large enough.
